# Audit cross block

A long note whose searched-for phrase sits well below the opening, so a
result that does not scroll is visibly a result that did not arrive.

The ruby sentence at the foot is the second case. The page draws its reading
in among the characters it is spoken over, so that block never names the words
a match follows and its term has to stand on its own — and a term standing
alone is looked for only where a word begins and where one ends. Searching for
the tail of the long word in it is therefore a search that used to arrive
nowhere.

The ledger opens on a quiet morning and nothing of consequence is written down.

A second reading of the same column finds the totals agreeing with themselves.

The clerk rules a fresh line and dates it, as the house style has long required.

Nothing in the margin suggests the day will be remembered for any reason at all.

A visitor asks after the older volumes and is shown the shelf behind the desk.

The shelf holds thirty years of similar mornings, bound in the same grey cloth.

Rain arrives in the afternoon and the window is closed against it without comment.

The totals are carried forward, and the carried figure is initialled in the usual place.

A telephone call interrupts the count and the count is begun again from the top.

The second count agrees with the first, which is recorded as a matter of routine.

Lamps are lit early because the sky has gone the colour of wet slate outside.

The junior is sent for more ink and returns with the wrong colour, as usual.

Black is found in the drawer where it has always been, under the spare nibs.

The page is turned and the new page is ruled exactly like the one before it.

Somebody has left a pencil mark near the foot of the column, and it is erased.

The erasure leaves a faint grey smudge that nobody thinks worth mentioning.

A cart passes in the street and the glass rattles once in its old frame.

The count resumes and the figures behave, which is not always how they behave.

Tea is brought at four and drunk at half past, by which time it has gone cold.

The ledger is squared away and the day's total is written in the outer column.

A correction from last week is found and entered, dated properly to the day made.

The house rule is that a correction is never scraped out, only written beside.

This rule has survived three owners and outlived every clerk who complained of it.

The window is opened again once the rain stops and the room smells of wet stone.

An audit is mentioned in passing and nobody looks up from what they are doing.

The mention is repeated the following morning and this time the room goes quiet.

Papers are gathered, and the older volumes come down off the shelf behind the desk.

Dust is wiped from the grey cloth with a cloth kept for exactly that purpose.

The auditor is expected on Thursday and the desk is cleared on Wednesday evening.

Thursday arrives with no rain and the light through the window is unusually even.

The auditor reads it aloud and the ledger entry closes with alpha

beta

gamma opens the column that the afternoon's correction belongs to.

The volumes go back on the shelf and the grey cloth is dusted a second time.

Friday opens on a quiet morning and nothing of consequence is written down.

The ledger entry closes with lanthanum here.
